newsitem.title: UK: Natwest says 5 leave after options loss.
newsitem.headline: Natwest says 5 leave after options loss.

text.p: National Westminster Bank Plc on Thursday confirmed that losses in its interest rate options trading will be 77 million pounds and that they were confined to that business.

Five senior staff in its investment banking unit NatWest Markets have resigned after it was found that the losses went undiscovered due to deliberate concealment and control weakness and that trader Kyriacos Papouis, who left NatWest in December 1996 covered up losses and created false profits over two years.

The report into the losses, first discovered in February, by law firm Linklaters & Paines and accountants Coopers & Lybrand, found that the losses in mark and sterling interest rate options had been due to poor trading and adverse market conditions.
The losses were then covered up, by deliberate mis-pricing and over-valuing of options contracts.

But NatWest said the full report is not being published for legal and commercial reasons, although it had been sent to the Bank of England and City regulator the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA). The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) had also been fully briefed, it added.

Those resigning from NatWest Markets include Neil Dodgson, who was global head of interest rate options, Jean-Francois Nguyen, global head of swaps and derivatives and Ian Gaskell, head of swaps and options trading.

Andrew Grout, manager of the London position-keeping team, has also resigned as a result of findings that he failed in his duty to alert senior management to unusual positions and transactions, NatWest said.
Philip Wise, head of debt capital markets from November 1995 to December 1996, has also accepted responsibility and resigned, but will be compensated for the term of his contract.

Gaskell will complete a three-month notice period and will receive no further compensation while Nguyen, Dodgson and Grout will receive no payment. The head of rate risk management, Christophe Lanson, is to leave the company but "is not considered to be responsible for the losses and false profits", NatWest said.
